svg.text: taia.ds — a component is a flow

g.text: {"count": 1,
{"count": 2,
send-event!
[:INCREMENT {}] + {:count 1}
ctx {:memory {:count 2}}
<div id="counter1"> … 2 …
server event
you write this
you write this
You write two things: a controller and a view
The controller is a state machine of plain functions; the view is a render fn, ctx → hiccup.
taia.ds does the rest: the route, finding your two namespaces, the flow and its chans, the signals, the morph.
A component is a flow
Two procs between an in-chan and an out-chan: the controller runs the state machine, the view renders.
Both are found once, when the flow is built; every event then travels the same wires.
A click puts an event on the in-chan
The POST carries the event and the component's signals: [:INCREMENT {}] with {:count 1 :state "displayed"}.
The controller runs the state machine
:INCREMENT → (increment ctx {}) → :memory {:count 2}.
Nothing is kept: the next event starts again from what the page sends.
The new ctx goes to the view
One connection inside the flow: the controller's :to-view feeds the view's :from-controller.
The view renders
(counter ctx) → hiccup: the new count, and the signals the page will send back next time.
Out of the out-chan, into the page
Datastar morphs #counter1 by id, and the signals now hold {:count 2}.
A one-shot component's flow stops here: every click builds its own.
A connected component's flow stays up
It lives as long as the page's SSE stream: (ds/send-event! cid user "tick" {:remaining 4}) puts a
server event, with its params, on the same in-chan; its render goes out the same way, down the stream.
